title: Status page
brief: When a big service has a problem, millions of people open its status page to see what is happening. The page must stay up exactly when everything else is down, and it must not share a home with the thing it reports on. A few staff update it by hand.

clarify.q: How fresh must the page be?
clarify.a: About 30 seconds behind is fine. Staff updates do not need to appear instantly.

clarify.q: Can it live next to the main service?
clarify.a: It should not. If the main region fails, the status page has to keep working.

clarify.q: How many people write to it?
clarify.a: A handful of staff. Almost all traffic is reading.

requirements.users: 5 million visitors in a bad week (approx.)
notes: The whole page is a few kilobytes of text (approx.).
During a big outage reads can be 5 times the usual (approx.).

numbers.label: Reads per second in a 5 times crowd
Page size
numbers.how: A small page of text and a few icons (approx.)

hints: Everyone reads the same page. How many of those reads must reach your own servers?
A CDN can keep the page for 30 seconds. Even a whole zone failing will not matter if the edge holds a copy.
CDN with a 30 second copy, load balancer over three zones, a few servers and a key-value store.

editorial.summary: One small page read by millions is the easiest thing to cache. A CDN holds it for about 30 seconds, so the servers see a handful of requests no matter how big the crowd. The rest is keeping the origin spread over zones.

designs.name: Edge copy with a spread-out origin
designs.why: The CDN answers nearly every read and collapses misses, so a 5 times crowd barely reaches the origin. Servers and the store sit in three zones, so one zone failing is invisible.

tradeoffs: A 30 second copy is slightly stale. Anything shorter costs more origin traffic with little gain.
Hosting away from the main service means a second set of accounts to look after, but it survives the failure you are reporting.
Serving a saved copy while the origin is down keeps the page up even in a full region outage.
Pay-per-request CDN pricing makes a 5 times crowd cost more, but only for the day it lasts.
editorial.realWorld: Status pages for big services are served almost entirely from an edge network. In a major incident, traffic can jump from a few requests a second to thousands within minutes (approx.).
